title: A fine vintage: L’Eroica sportive
content:
Cyclist
A fine vintage: L’Eroica sportive

Just for today you can forget your wind-tunnel-optimised aero frameset, your high-modulus carbon layup and 3D printed saddle. L’Eroica operates a strict door policy, where only bikes made before 1988 have access to the start line of this self-proclaimed ‘cycling history event’. Article 6.1.a of the rules further stipulates that bikes must feature down tube shifters, external brake cables and wheel rims no deeper than 20mm. Modern Lycra jerseys are not permitted, and don’t even think about using clipless pedals.

‘I am not fascinated by the past because I think it was better,’ says L’Eroica’s founder, Giancarlo Brocci. ‘I am fascinated by it because it was more essential. The riders had simple equipment so they had to rely on their own determination to overcome every difficulty. The relationship between the rider and the bicycle was direct, with very little in between. Technological progress is a wonderful achievement but it can never replace character, patience or the willingness to embrace effort and fatigue.’

Brocci is obviously not the only one who feels this way. The L’Eroica franchise he created now comprises a dozen events, with editions as far away as Japan and South Africa, but the original is still the greatest, and it returns each year to the gravel roads surrounding Gaiole in Chianti, located some 30km west of Siena.

‘Gaiole is where everything began,’ Brocci continues. ‘There is a unique relationship here between the people and the landscape. The white roads have always been part of the history of these hills, but when thousands of cyclists arrive from every continent, they are welcomed not as customers but as guests.’

The details

What L’Eroica
Where Gaiole in Chiante, Italy
How far 132km (2,300m elevation). Other options include 45km, 82km, 100km or 210km
Surface 40% gravel, 60% paved
Next event 3rd October 2026
How much €100 (approx £85)
More info eroica.cc

Essential riding

It’s well before breakfast when I arrive in Gaiole and track down the early ’80s Ciocc bike that I have been loaned for the 132km ride. I strap a bag filled with biscotti and spare tubes to its yellow handlebars and make my way to the start line, shivering in the chilly 6am temperature.

The Tuscan village remains cloaked in darkness by the time my wave gets underway and rolls out southward. I’m glad to be moving to get some warmth into my exposed limbs, while around me riders begin shedding the various layers of clothing that have helped them get through the long, cold wait in the starting pen.

By the time I get the hang of my down tube shifters, the sun is beginning to rise over the terracotta-coloured Castello di Brolio. The grounds of this 16th century castle offer our first taste of the white roads, and to mark the occasion the gravel tilts up to gradients close to 10%. At its crest I find myself inside a Renaissance painting: orange sky, cypress trees, vineyards, castle turrets and the wispy outline of the Tuscan hills on the horizon.

It feels rude to interrupt the serenity but there’s something romantic about the wool jerseys, leather helmets and flat-soled shoes occupying some space in the frame. Back in the saddle, however, that bliss is quickly offset by the ride’s first gravel descent, where my skinny tyres barely offer the traction necessary to shoot through the vineyards towards the bottom of that vista.

At this point I’m neatly embedded in a peloton until my rear tyre starts to rub against the seatstay and I’m forced to stop. The moment I unclip, a man in a boiler suit sporting a finely tuned moustache attempts to resolve the issue, which works until I clunk into the big ring and the wheel jolts once more. I could spend valuable time tinkering with it on the roadside, but I soon accept that it’s not a bad thing to be on a primitive 1x setup on a course as hilly as this.

Thankfully, most of this sector is downhill but the dust being kicked up by a mechanic’s motorbike makes it wheezier than I would have wanted. Once we get off the gravel I give my specs a good scrub and notice the road signs directing us to Siena.

Our entrance is much less punchy than the Via Santa Caterina in the finale of Strade Bianche, yet here I am panting up the Via Pantaneto at the same pace as a gaggle of tourists who seem confused by the sight of a bunch of cyclists who have apparently arrived from a different century.

I’m directed left to meet the Palazzo Pubblico’s 102m-tall belfry, which guards the bowl-shaped Piazza del Campo, venue for both the finish of Strade Bianche and the medieval Palio horse race. There’s less cavalry and more Campagnolo in the Piazza today, but the vintage kit of the riders seems perfectly at home against this timeless backdrop.

Article continues below…

Sterrato and fiasco

After feasting on pastries and Nutella we leave Siena from stage right, taking us on a steep descent through the narrow streets. Not far beyond the city’s Roman Gate, the tarmac runs out near Colle Malamerenda. This gravel sector is long at 12km, relentlessly undulating and, by this point in the morning, exposed to the Italian sunshine.

As we navigate the dusty sterrato the scene looks like something from an era I have only learned about through black and white films and descriptions in L’Équipe. Add in the backdrop of the endless Tuscan hills and this is precisely the experience I had expected from a ‘cycling history event’. Riders sporting casquettes labour over leather-wrapped bars while vintage Fiat 500s kick up clouds of dirt that cake the jerseys and faces of the peloton. I’m half expecting to see Fausto Coppi appear out of the dust.

The re-emergence of tarmac soon breaks this delusion and the road rises to meet the village of Murlo, which is only accessible today by a steep 300m stretch of singletrack. It’s worth the squeeze, however, as it seems we have arrived in a medieval village cryogenically frozen in time, with its ivy-wrapped walls and narrow streets. They’ve even brought out some locals dressed as noblemen.

A queue leads to the feed stop where there’s not a protein bar or energy gel in sight – rather we gorge on bean soups, apricot crostata, gnocchi and enough olive oil to keep the calorie stores high after 55km in the legs. If that wasn’t enough, I’m then offered a bulbous bottle of red wine, several litres in capacity, wrapped in some sort of wicker. The bottle is apparently called a fiasco, which seems fitting given the crush of riders waving plastic cups to get their share of the local tipple.

By the time it reaches my cup it’s already on the warm side, but who am I to complain? It makes a nice change from the isotonic drink that’s usually on offer at sportive feed stops, and once I’ve drained my cup I saddle up and begin to skirt the route’s southern flank.

After Murlo the sterrato becomes a near constant for the following 50km. So having indulged in my previous visions of Coppian grandeur, it’s now more a matter of getting my head down and ticking off some kilometres to reach the next bowl of nonna’s bean soup.

Along the roadside sit riders battling to prise tyres off dusty clincher wheels or coax ancient groupsets back into life. For many of them the ride might end up in the back of the ominous pickup truck weaving through the white roads, scooping up the fallen.

Crunch time

While L’Eroica is all about the historical side of cycling, it provided the blueprint for the modern Strade Bianche WorldTour race. The events share a few sectors, but the Monte Sante Marie is by far the most emblematic to feature on both parcours, having been used as Tadej Pogačar’s launchpad to victory no fewer than four times, in 2022 and in each of the past three editions.

Despite its monte name, this 11km sector is punishingly rolling and punctuated by sketchy descents during its first two-thirds. With my bike still miraculously in one piece after some close calls, I make contact with the business end of the Monte Sante Marie, a stretch made to look easy by the Slovenian champion.

Easy it certainly isn’t, as the gravel track wiggles up slopes well above 10% during its brief kilometre-long classified ascent. Throw in the slippery road surface and it’s hard to imagine how Pogačar manages to lay his yearly attack on this pitch.

As I glance back, it looks like a string of ants making its way up this sliver of dust. There’s no shame in pushing a bike up here. After all, Brocci told me last night that one of L’Eroica’s core values was ‘the pleasure of doing things at our own pace’.

Eventually I make it to the sticker-covered summit sign with my handlebars slathered in a mix of sweat, dust and sun cream. My reward is a final supper in Castelnuovo Bardegna before setting sights on the final 30km with one last crostata to burn off. To my tyres’ relief, the Monte Santa Marie was something of a show-closer for the sterrato and the route sticks to tarmac from here on out.

Even still, with the fatigue of the past 100km, the approach is far from simple. There are some fast descents but more importantly a slog of a climb to the Castello di Brolio, where we started the gravelled challenge about ten hours ago.

Knowing Gaiole is near, we begin to exchange handshakes within the grupetto I’ve become familiarised with over the past 10km. Some link arms or unfurl flags, but all absorb the cheers and applause as we enter this little village adorned with woollen cycling jerseys and L’Eroica bunting.

‘Gaiole is where everything began,’ Brocci told me before the event. ‘You’ll remember the challenge of the route, but even more a smile at a food stop, a conversation in the village or a family cheering from the side of the road. L’Eroica is an international event with the heart of a small village.’

Once I cross the line and get handed my medal and a cup of Chianti, his words start to ring true. This really is just a village fête that got a bit out of hand.

‘The spirit of L’Eroica’

How a village get-together became an international phenomenon

‘L’Eroica was never created to become successful,’ founder Giancarlo Brocci tells Cyclist. ‘It began as the passion project of friends who wanted to save the white roads, vintage bicycles and the memory of heroic cycling.

‘The spirit of Eroica began with a simple question: what from our past is worth preserving to help us live better in the future? Over time we realised we were also preserving the beauty of fatigue, respect for the landscape and the pleasure of doing things at our own pace. Today Eroica still speaks about the past, but not out of nostalgia. In a world that is constantly accelerating, choosing to slow down can be a profoundly contemporary act.

‘Perhaps Eroica has endured because we have never tried to follow trends. We have simply tried to remain faithful to our identity while the world around us keeps changing.’
